title: TSMC reportedly demands cash up front from AI chip clients amid circular financing fears
summary: If confirmed, the move would be a vote of caution about AI customer finances from the company with the clearest view of chip demand. That would add weight to the circular financing debate that has hung over AI stocks this month. Summary: TSMC is reportedly setting credit limits for customers based on their balance sheets, payment history and default risk Orders above the limit must reportedly be paid in cash, and some customers must prepay to secure capacity The policy mainly affects custom AI chip makers, several of which are raising money through bonds, equity and loans The report links the change to concerns about circular financing in AI TSMC has not announced the policy, and the outlet could not confirm it independently TSMC has begun weighing customers’ finances before handing out chipmaking capacity, setting credit limits and asking some buyers to pay cash up front, Chinese technology outlet Kuai Keji reported,
body: If confirmed, the move would be a vote of caution about AI customer finances from the company with the clearest view of chip demand. That would add weight to the circular financing debate that has hung over AI stocks this month. Custom chip designers and smaller AI players with stretched balance sheets would face tighter cash flow and could lose capacity to better-funded rivals. For TSMC, the policy would strengthen its pricing power and reduce its credit risk, a positive for the stock and for Taiwan’s tech-heavy market. Watch for any confirmation or denial from TSMC, which would set how seriously the report is taken. While Nvidia extends credit to the AI boom, TSMC is reportedly asking its customers to show the money first, and that difference says a lot about who carries the risk. TSMC has begun weighing customers’ finances before handing out chipmaking capacity, setting credit limits and asking some buyers to pay cash up front, Chinese technology outlet Kuai Keji reported, citing industry sources. TSMC has not announced the policy, and the outlet said it could not independently confirm it. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, or TSMC, is the world’s largest contract chipmaker. It does not design its own chips. Instead, it manufactures them for companies such as Nvidia, Apple, AMD and the growing number of firms building custom AI processors. Founded in Hsinchu in 1987, it produces the vast majority of the world’s most advanced chips. That gives it near-monopoly control of the capacity every AI company needs, and that leverage is what lets it set terms on who gets served first. According to the report, TSMC now sets a credit limit for each customer based on its balance sheet. The assessment reportedly covers any history of late or unpaid bills, the customer’s standing in the industry, its business outlook and the estimated loss if it defaulted. Orders above that limit must be paid in cash, and some customers must prepay to secure their allocated capacity. The change is said to apply mainly to makers of custom AI chips, several of which are raising money through overseas convertible bonds, equity sales and syndicated bank loans. The report links the shift directly to concerns about circular financing in the AI industry, where companies invest in one another and then buy from each other. In effect, TSMC would be moving from allocating capacity on a first-come, first-served basis to asking customers to prove they can pay. That fits with comments from chief executive C.C. Wei, who has said on an earnings call that capacity planning takes into account cloud providers’ capital spending, their financial condition, and the availability of power and components. TSMC has also sent staff to the United States to check on data centre construction. The company already holds large customer prepayments, around NT$234 billion at the end of June, although Kuai Keji noted these are standard accounting prepayments rather than the new credit system. The contrast with Nvidia is striking. Nvidia is increasingly acting as a financier of the AI build-out, with commitments of about $518 billion and customer receivables of about $81 billion, according to its latest results and a Financial Times report. TSMC, sitting further up the supply chain with near-monopoly control of advanced chipmaking, appears to be heading the other way, shifting risk back onto its customers. If confirmed, the policy would tighten cash flow for chip designers that already tie up large sums in design and packaging costs, and it would favour well-funded customers over smaller players. It would also be a sign that the company best placed to judge AI demand wants protection in case some of its customers cannot pay. Your market education doesn't end here. body: Tokenized equities are still far too small to move BTC or ETH. The read-through is for listed crypto names tied to the sector, including Robinhood as an issuer and Coinbase as a venue for tokenized assets, and for the wider real-world asset story. If Nvidia’s post-earnings gains hold, most of the tokens minted near $156 will be in profit. That would help issuers argue that onchain demand rises with volatility instead of evaporating. The risk is redemptions into strength, which would shrink supply as quickly as it grew and weaken the case for tokenized stocks as a lasting home for retail risk appetite. While Wall Street sold Nvidia’s leadership crisis, onchain buyers minted more than a million new tokenized shares, and Kress’s first earnings beat gave them an early reason to feel good about it. Holders of tokenized Nvidia stock added to their positions as the chipmaker’s shares fell through the week of Jensen Huang’s resignation, with onchain supply rising 121% to about 2.3 million tokens, according to Token Terminal data shared by Token Relations. Over the same seven days, Nvidia’s share price dropped 13% to around $156. The timing also stands out. The data show supply starting to climb around November 9 and 10, after Nvidia’s board announced an independent investigation on November 8 and before the November 12 announcement that Huang had stepped down as president, chief executive and director. Chief financial officer Colette Kress was named interim CEO, and Harvey C. Jones became the company’s first board chair. Most of the new supply came through bStocks’ NVDAb token, with xStocks’ NVDAx, Robinhood’s version and 15 smaller tokens making up the rest. Those buyers got an early test of their conviction overnight. As we reported, Kress’s first quarterly report since Huang’s departure topped forecasts by about $7 billion, and she pointed to a $2.5 trillion backlog while guiding for revenue growth of around 75% next year. Nvidia shares rose in after-hours trading. The episode offers a rare look at how onchain equity holders behave during a single-stock shock. The sums are small beside Nvidia’s market value of several trillion dollars, but the direction is clear: demand for tokenized exposure rose as the price fell. The next few sessions will show whether that was conviction or a short-term trade. If supply holds or keeps growing after the post-earnings bounce, issuers will have evidence that volatility brings in buyers. If holders redeem into strength, the surge will look more like a quick dip trade than a lasting shift. as a ps. if there is any demand for it I'll post up a separate explainer on all this. body: The Australian dollar barely moved, holding around 0.67, because traders treated the data as backward-looking and are focused on Thursday’s jobs report. Swaps still lean towards a peak in rates. A firm jobs number would challenge that, lifting front-end yields and supporting the currency, while a rise in unemployment would reinforce bets on easing by 2027. The contrast between strong wage growth and rising layoffs creates two-way risk for Australian bank stocks and rate-sensitive retailers, especially given the job cuts at David Jones and Bunnings. Watch the jobless rate on Thursday more closely than the headline jobs figure. --- Australia now has wages, interest rates and unemployment all rising together, which leaves the RBA choosing between the pay data and the layoff headlines. Australian wages grew at their fastest pace in nearly three years in the September quarter, giving the Reserve Bank of Australia more reason to keep policy tight even as cracks appear in the jobs market. The Australian Bureau of Statistics said its wage price index rose 1.1% in the quarter, the strongest result since late 2023. That broke a run of five quarters at around 0.8% and topped forecasts of between 0.9% and 1.0%. Annual growth picked up to 3.5% from 3.2%. Private sector pay rose 3.4% over the year and public sector pay 3.9%, Reuters reported. The ABS pointed to two drivers. The Fair Work Commission’s 4.75% increase in minimum and award wages from July lifted private sector pay, while raises for state government frontline workers pushed up public sector wages. Public sector pay has now outpaced the private sector for seven straight quarters. Real wages are still going backwards, down 0.4% over the year, the fourth consecutive quarter of decline. For the RBA, the harder question is what it may take to bring inflation down. If pay keeps rising at this rate, the bank may have to tolerate a jobless rate higher than it currently projects, possibly above the level it regards as consistent with steady inflation. The central bank has argued that the labour market is easing, yet pay growth shows little sign of cooling broadly. And unless productivity picks up, wage gains of this size sit uneasily with inflation returning to the 2% to 3% band. For households, at least, bigger pay rises offer some relief after a long squeeze. The bank lifted rates for a fifth time this year in November, to an 18-year high of 4.85%, partly because it judged the labour market to be a little tight. Three board members opposed the move, concerned the economy could be heading for a materially sharper downturn. One economist noted that Australia is in the unusual position of having unemployment, interest rates and wages all rising at once, and said wage growth and joblessness are likely to stay elevated through 2027. There are signs that the labour market is weakening. Unemployment hit a five-year high of 4.7% in September, and layoffs are spreading. Department store David Jones plans to cut 1,500 jobs by the end of the year, and hardware chain Bunnings said this week it would cut around 230 permanent roles. That puts Thursday’s employment report in focus. Forecasts point to a rise of 25,000 jobs in October and an unchanged unemployment rate of 4.7%. Markets largely looked through the wage figures, treating them as backward-looking. Swaps still imply about a 75% chance that the RBA has finished raising rates, with roughly 20 basis points of easing priced by the end of 2027. A strong jobs report on Thursday would test that confidence, while a weak one would strengthen the case of the three dissenters. Your market education doesn't end here. body: Record exports support the view that Japan’s economy can absorb a December rate hike despite the third-quarter contraction, which should keep upward pressure on short-end JGB yields. Chipmakers and chip equipment suppliers in Tokyo are the clearest beneficiaries, though the reliance on AI demand leaves them exposed to any pullback in global tech spending. Oil is the swing factor for the trade balance: crude prices tied to the Iran war set the size of Japan’s import bill, and a renewed spike would quickly widen the deficit. The yen is likely to take its direction from US-Japan rate gaps rather than the trade figures. --- Japan is selling more than ever to an AI-hungry world, but record oil-driven import costs mean households are not sharing in the boom. Japan’s exports rose for a 14th straight month in October and hit a record value, as global investment in artificial intelligence kept demand for chip-related shipments strong, Ministry of Finance data showed on Wednesday. Exports climbed 20.5% from a year earlier to about ¥11.8 trillion, roughly $74 billion and the highest for any single month on record, Reuters reported. That beat the 20% median forecast and picked up from September’s 16.5% gain. Shipments to the United States rose about 24%, while exports to China increased about 13%. Analysts cited by Reuters said AI-related demand continued to support exports of semiconductors and chipmaking equipment, helping offset sluggish Chinese demand. Economists also noted that companies passing on higher costs had lifted the nominal value of shipments, so part of the gain reflects prices rather than volumes. Imports also set a monthly record at about ¥12.2 trillion, up 21.6% from a year earlier, although that was below the 25.8% forecast. Elevated crude prices and higher transport costs pushed up the value of energy imports amid instability in the Middle East, even as import volumes slipped 0.2%. Oil remains Japan’s main exposure to the Iran war, since the country imports close to 90% of its energy. The softer than expected import bill left a trade deficit of around ¥477 billion, about half the shortfall economists had forecast. The data shows external demand is still supporting an economy that contracted unexpectedly in the third quarter, as higher living costs forced households to cut spending. Rising import costs are likely to keep squeezing household purchasing power and corporate margins, which means the export boom is not translating into broad domestic strength. For the Bank of Japan, the figures add to the case for raising rates in December. Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Wednesday that the bank will keep raising its policy rate in line with economic, price and financial developments, and that financial conditions remain accommodative. The policy rate is 1.25%. Resilient exports help offset the weak GDP reading, while import-driven inflation keeps pressure on the bank to act. The yen has drawn little support so far. USD/JPY remains near 160, where Tokyo has warned about intervention, as the rate gap with a Federal Reserve on a hiking path dominates. The risks to the export run are a slowdown in AI investment and further escalation in the Middle East, which would lift the oil import bill again. Your market education doesn't end here. body: The narrower deficit is mildly supportive for the yen because it reduces the yen sold to pay for imports. Rate differentials still dominate, though, and USD/JPY remains pinned near 160 while the Fed is on a hiking path. Oil is the key swing factor: Japan’s import bill is highly sensitive to crude prices during the Iran war, so any renewed rise in oil would quickly reverse today’s improvement. For the BOJ, the data adds to evidence that the economy can absorb a December hike, which could nudge short-end JGB yields higher. Exporters with heavy chip exposure should find support in Tokyo trade. Chips lifted Japan’s exports and a lighter import bill halved the expected trade gap, but the yen is still taking its cue from Washington, not Tokyo. Japan’s exports rose 20.5% in October from a year earlier, slightly ahead of expectations and a clear pick-up from September’s revised 16.5%, Ministry of Finance data showed on Wednesday. Chip shipments led the gain, ending a two-month slowdown in export growth. Imports rose 21.6%, well short of forecasts of about 26%, after an 18.5% rise in September. As a result, the trade deficit came in at around ¥477 billion. That was roughly half the ¥1 trillion or so analysts had expected and narrower than September’s revised ¥557 billion. On a seasonally adjusted basis, the deficit was around ¥767 billion, smaller than forecast but wider than the previous month. The import figure is the surprise. The government had said crude procurement would recover in October to around year-earlier levels as tankers routed through the Suez Canal arrived, so a bigger jump in the import bill was widely expected. Energy is Japan’s main vulnerability in the Iran war. The country imports close to 90% of its energy, and high oil prices have kept its import bill elevated. The data adds a modest tailwind to the Bank of Japan’s case for raising rates in December. The central bank held its policy rate at 1.25% in October, but Governor Kazuo Ueda signalled strong prospects for a hike at the next meeting after declaring that underlying inflation had reached the 2% target. Board member Hajime Takata said this week that rates should rise nimbly. Solid exports help offset a slight contraction in third-quarter GDP, and a narrower trade deficit means fewer yen are being sold to pay for imports. That may not be enough to lift the yen on its own. USD/JPY is trading around 159.5, just below the 160 level where Tokyo has stepped up warnings about intervention. With the Federal Reserve on a hiking path and US 10-year yields above 5%, the rate gap still works against the yen even if the Bank of Japan hikes. The 10-year JGB yield is near 2.9%, close to its highest since late October. The next test is Friday’s national inflation data. A firm reading alongside today’s trade figures would strengthen expectations for a December move. A rise in oil prices, on the other hand, would quickly push the import bill and the deficit back up. body: Alex Kimani is a veteran finance writer, investor, engineer and researcher for Safehaven.com. We are currently at the tail-end of the third quarter earnings season, with more than 90% of S&P 500 companies having reported, and it’s proven to be yet another bumper season. According to FactSet data , the index has reported 31.9% Y/Y average earnings growth, marking the third consecutive quarter that earnings growth has exceeded 25%. All 11 sectors of the U.S. market have posted positive earnings and revenue growth, with seven reporting double-digit earnings growth led by the energy, IT and materials sectors. The energy sector has posted the highest earnings growth amongst the 11 sectors at 151.2% Y/Y as well as the second-highest revenue growth at 35.7% Y/Y, thanks to higher energy prices. Oil prices averaged $85.68/bbl in the third quarter, ~32% higher compared to the corresponding quarter a year ago. At the sub-industry level, 4 of the 5 sub-industries in the energy sector have reported positive earnings growth led by Oil & Gas Refining & Marketing (542%), Integrated Oil & Gas (141%), Oil & Gas Exploration & Production (83%), and Oil & Gas Storage & Transportation (30%). Only the Oil & Gas Equipment & Services (-3%) sub-industry has reported a decline in earnings. Here are 5 Oil & Gas Companies that have easily exceeded Wall Street expectations: Record Permian Basin volumes lifted ONEOK’s (NYSE:OKE) third-quarter earnings, and the Tulsa-based pipeline operator is raising its spending to add processing, pipeline and export capacity in the Permian and on the Gulf Coast. ONEOK gathers, processes, transports and stores natural gas, natural gas liquids (NGLs), refined products and crude oil across a 60,000-mile network linking producers to domestic and international markets. NGL raw feed throughput rose 6% to nearly 1.7 million barrels per day, with the Gulf Coast/Permian region up 16%. Refined products shipments climbed 6% and Permian gas processing volumes rose 4%. Those gains raised adjusted EBITDA 6% year-over-year to $2.24 billion. ONEOK’s headline earnings of $2.13 per diluted share beat the consensus by 63 cents, though 53 cents of that came from a one-time, non-cash tax benefit tied to a corporate reorganization. Stripped of the benefit, the company still beat consensus by a dime. Management raised full-year guidance for the third time this year, citing record Permian volumes and the Permian Midland assets ONEOK bought from Brazos Midstream. The adjusted EBITDA midpoint rose by 200 million dollars to $8.55 billion, and the company now expects earnings of 6.30 dollars per diluted share at the midpoint. ONEOK raised its 2026 capital budget to about $3.5 billion from 3.2 billion to speed up construction of the Cutter II processing plant and a Delaware Basin NGL expansion. That expansion will add 245,000 barrels per day of takeaway capacity in the third quarter of 2027. ONEOK is also expanding its export capacity. Volumes at its Galena Park export terminal rose about 15% in the quarter, and a 400,000-barrel-per-day LPG export terminal at Texas City is due in early 2028. Occidental Petroleum (NYSE:OXY) cut its principal debt to $10 billion in the third quarter, reaching that target ahead of schedule . The Houston-based oil and gas producer repaid 1.8 billion dollars of principal in the quarter and 10.4 billion so far this year, after closing the sale of OxyChem , its chemicals business, to Berkshire Hathaway in January. Production averaged 1.43 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, 7,000 above the midpoint of guidance. Adjusted earnings of $1.91 per share beat Wall Street’s consensus of 1.34 by 57 cents, and free cash flow reached about 2.8 billion dollars, the highest since 2022. body: Sentiment in the crypto market stayed muted on Tuesday, even as Nvidia's (NVDA) Q3 results surpassed analysts' forecasts. Continued demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure underpinned growth across the company's business. Record results were announced by the AI chipmaker, with third-quarter revenue at $115.8 billion, representing growth of 103% YoY and 20% over the preceding quarter. At $65.3 billion, net income also set a record, rising 9% QoQ and 105% from a year earlier. Revenue from Nvidia's Data Center division climbed 110% year-on-year to $107.6 billion, maintaining its position as the company's biggest revenue contributor. GAAP diluted earnings per share came in at $2.70. For the fourth quarter, Nvidia projects revenue of approximately $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, above analysts' forecasts. Colette Kress, Nvidia's interim CEO, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, said: “Our roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater,” The earnings announcement prompted little price response from leading cryptocurrencies Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH) and XRP. AI-linked tokens, by contrast, registered modest gains, with leading names in the category moving into positive territory for the day. Among them, Near Protocol (NEAR) advanced 3.4% over the past 24 hours following the announcement. Gains in Bittensor (TAO), Venice (VVV), Render (RENDER) and Pearl (PEARL) stood at 0.8%, 1.3%, 2.7% and 8%, respectively. Weakness in AI shares formed the backdrop to the earnings release. Nvidia has also been in focus following last week's resignation of co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang. Before Huang stepped down, revelations about his personal life had emerged, and Nvidia's board had launched an independent investigation into concerns over a reported foreign intelligence effort targeting him. On Tuesday, however, Huang ended his silence through a message on social media platform X. He acknowledged his mistakes and indicated that he was willing to rejoin the company if the board deemed it appropriate. In his words: "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," His remarks coincide with Nvidia's leadership transition under Colette Kress, who serves as interim CEO as well as chief financial officer. According to Huang, many employees and investors are urging him to resume leadership of the company. Huang outlined his position: “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” After ending Tuesday's session 0.6% lower, NVDA is trading 3.8% higher after hours following the earnings announcement. Having broken key support at $165, the stock encounters heavy resistance on rebounds. TradingKey - Nvidia surged 4% after hours, but dim prospects of Jensen Huang's return cap valuations, and potential Fed rate hikes could drag the stock down toward the $100 mark. After the bell on November 17, Eastern Time, AI giant Nvidia ( NVDA ) reported its fiscal 2027 third-quarter results, delivering an across-the-board beat that drove its after-hours stock price up more than 4% to surge to $163, before pulling back to around $157. Nvidia's latest earnings report showed that both quarterly revenue and data center revenue surpassed the $100 billion mark, while its fourth-quarter revenue guidance significantly beat Wall Street consensus, directly dispelling market concerns over a slowdown in AI computing capital expenditures. Beat expectations, up 103.1% year over year, topping the $100 billion mark for the first time in history Beat expectations, AI computing hardware demand maintains strong momentum Above expectations across the board, dispelling market concerns over a slowdown in AI capex Nvidia's better-than-expected results and guidance demonstrate that the company still possesses strong momentum in operational execution, supply chain delivery, and customer relations, easing market panic over a leadership void. Although short-term fundamentals remain sound, Jensen Huang was Nvidia's soul and technological visionary; his departure and the board's stated lack of intention to bring him back have made some long-term institutional investors more cautious when assigning forward P/E multiples for the next 3 to 5 years. Until an official new CEO is named and proves their strategic leadership, it will be difficult for the market to grant Nvidia the extreme "leadership halo premium" of the past. As a result, the stock pulled back after rebounding on positive news, making it difficult to replicate past one-sided short squeezes with unlimited upside. Recently, both U.S. October inflation data (CPI/PPI) and retail sales data beat expectations, pushing 10-year Treasury yields firmly above 5%. The market has begun to reprice the risk of the Fed keeping interest rates higher for longer or even resuming rate hikes within the next 12 months. High risk-free rates directly compress the discounted value of future cash flows for high-growth tech stocks, triggering capital outflows from highly valued tech sectors, making it very likely that Nvidia's stock will face continued downward pressure. Nvidia's stock price has now broken below $165, a strong support level that held across multiple pullbacks from September 2025 to November 2026. It has now turned into strong resistance, hindering stock rebounds and meaning that every bounce is likely to attract break-even selling pressure and short-term profit-taking. On technical charts, when the stock recently fell toward $148–$150, it received short-term buying support that sparked an oversold rebound. However, if the macroeconomic environment continues to deteriorate and this defensive line is broken on heavy volume, technicals will open up room for further downside to seek deeper support, with the next dense trading zone of historical turnover significance sitting near $100. body: Nov 17 (Reuters) – Nvidia board Chairman Harvey Jones opened a conference call with investors on Tuesday by saying the AI chip company would not rehire co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO and would not take questions about his departure. Coming on top of strong results, Jones’ comments were a forceful response to a movement to bring back Huang, who stepped down last week. With Huang gone, investors are eager for clues about Nvidia’s future and strategy, from its commitments of billions of dollars to cloud providers, suppliers and ​AI startups to who will ultimately lead the world’s most valuable chipmaker. Jones said the board had hired executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to help find a new CEO. “We want to install the ‌CEO, the permanent CEO, as quickly as possible, but we won’t expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person,” he added. He was joined on the call by interim CEO Colette Kress, who is also finance chief, and engineer Ian Buck, the vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing. “Having the combination of Kress, Jones and Buck on the line was a smart move because it guaranteed that they were prepared to deal with financial, technical and high-level strategic questions. Plus, it was a necessary step towards showing the world a wider range of voices from within Nvidia,” said Bob O’Donnell, chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research. Shares of the company rose 4% in extended trading, after Nvidia forecast sales ahead of Wall Street targets. Still, the $3.8 trillion value of the company is down about $2 trillion ‌from an ​early October high. Kress defended her team’s work since Huang’s departure. “Our leadership has stood up so strongly over the last week,” she said. “We’ve got this.” Leadership ⁠from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, which makes chips for Nvidia, was ⁠in the office and “fully engaged in helping us,” she said. In prepared remarks she added that the company’s latest flagship AI chip, called Vera Rubin, was off to an explosive start. Shares of specialized AI cloud providers CoreWeave, Nebius, IREN and Applied Digital extended gains after Kress told analysts that while the chipmaker has conditions on its investments, it has made no changes to how it backs its neocloud commitments. Huang, widely regarded as a public face of the AI boom, resigned on Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang and two with Nvidia employees. US intelligence agencies are trying to ​determine the extent of Alice Huang’s ties to China’s Ministry of State Security and what information she may have passed to Beijing, according to two people familiar with the matter. China has rejected allegations of an espionage operation targeting Jensen Huang. The US Securities and Exchange Commission is probing Nvidia after Huang’s resignation as CEO last week, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday afternoon. The SEC declined to comment. Huang’s exit ended three decades of ⁠founder-led control over Nvidia’s chip roadmap, customer deals and Washington ties, making execution a bigger risk than near-term AI demand, analysts said. ⁠The absence of Huang, a gregarious CEO, also contributed to a much shorter earnings conference call, which ended in under an hour. “It’s no surprise that they’re doing ​very well, and there’ll be people who will breathe a sigh of relief about it,” said Rick Meckler, partner at Cherry Lane Investments. “But the story here is very complicated, and it’s hard not to factor that in as an ​additional risk for people buying stock.” The company expects fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, above analysts’ average estimate of $125.25 billion, according to LSEG ‌data. Nvidia said the outlook assumes no data-center chip sales to China. Adjusted gross margin is expected at 71% to 72%, compared with analysts’ estimate of 71.7%. title: Nvidia Signals AI Financing Flywheel Will Continue, But ‘Disciplined’: Analyst Calls Neoclouds Its ‘Biggest Sustained Bet’ As NBIS, IREN, MRVL Rally - Yahoo Finance
body: Nvidia reported Q3 results above expectations and raised its fiscal 2028 sales forecast. NBIS and IREN rose over 10% in overnight trading, while CRWV gained 9%. "The Neoclouds aren't a nice to have for $NVDA. It's the biggest sustained bet," said analyst Daniel Newman. Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) on Tuesday said it will continue supporting the AI infrastructure buildout through investments and credit guarantees, albeit with a "selective" and "disciplined" approach, easing a key concern AI investors had after former CEO Jensen Huang's exit. Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress highlighted neocloud operators as an important part of the AI chain and its continued support, but clarified that credit backstops activate only if partners can build and deliver the computing infrastructure. See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox Neocloud, AI infrastructure, and chip stocks rallied on the disclosures, buoyed by Nvidia's strong quarterly results and outlook. Nebius (NBIS) and IREN ltd. (IREN) rose over 10% in overnight trading late Tuesday, while CoreWeave (CRWV) gained 9%. Marvell Technology (MRVL) gained 5.7% and Arista Networks (ANET) rose 3.7%. Chip heavyweights Intel (INTC), Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), Micron (MU) and Broadcom (AVGO) rose 2.7% to 4.7%, pushing the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) 3.8% higher. "Neoclouds remain an increasingly important part of the global AI infrastructure ecosystem, providing additional customers with access to Nvidia compute and expanding the reach of our platform," Kress said on the analyst call. "We have supported the development of this ecosystem, and we will continue to be disciplined and selective in our support." Nvidia has become a de facto financier of AI infrastructure, partnering with and investing in dozens of companies. Huang played a central role in these deals, and his departure fueled concerns that Nvidia might scale back its support. "As we advance this work, we remain thoughtful in how we participate and disciplined in how we commit capital. We are proud of the role that we have played so far in supporting the ecosystem," Kress said. "As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments and guarantees," Kress said. Nvidia disclosed $32 billion in neocloud commitments, down from $36 billion in Q2, and $118 billion in total guarantees. The chipmaker reported $390 billion committed toward future supply and capacity, up from $279 billion a quarter ago. Nvidia said the uptick was "primarily related to the multiyear procurement of memory supply," the company said. "Beyond its impressive, consensus-beating revenue growth and profitability, Nvidia's quarterly earnings also highlight its expanding role as a major AI creditor and investor," Wharton professor Mohamed A. El-Erian said in an X post. Hedge fund manager Eric Jackson said Nvidia's push in AI infrastructure was the earnings' highlight: "When asked about future financing priorities, Colette Kress singled out the physical infrastructure needed to house AI compute." The Futurum Group CEO Daniel Newman said neocloud commitments are "critical" to Nvidia's growth. "The Neoclouds aren't a nice to have for $NVDA. It's the biggest sustained bet it has on creating an ecosystem of NVIDIA powered hyperscalers that won't look to build competitive or meaningfully augment with custom silicon." Nvidia's third-quarter revenue more than doubled to $115.8 billion, beating expectations of $109.3 billion. Sales from the all-important data center segment rose 110% to $107.6 billion, also higher than targets. Nvidia forecast $130 billion in revenue for the current quarter, about 4% higher than Wall Street estimates according to The Wall Street Journal.
